detail.title: What it is, and what it actually does
detail.lede: Magical Liquid is a buffered borate solution engineered to cross-link polyvinyl acetate — the polymer in ordinary white school glue — into a stable, elastic gel. That is the whole of slime chemistry, and this bottle is the whole of the recipe.

blocks.heading: One pour replaces three ingredients
blocks.body: The usual kitchen method asks for baking soda, contact lens solution and a lot of hope. Each is doing a separate job, and each is easy to get wrong — too little and the mix stays sticky, too much and it snaps like putty. Magical Liquid is pre-buffered, so the alkalinity and the cross-linker arrive together in the correct ratio. You pour, you stir, it works.
blocks.imageAlt: Close crop of the printed front label

blocks.heading: Consistent from the first batch to the last
blocks.body: Because the ratio is fixed in the bottle rather than in the bowl, batch two comes out like batch one. That matters more than it sounds: it is the difference between a classroom of thirty working slimes and a classroom of thirty different failures, and it is why this is the format we sell.
blocks.imageAlt: Close crop of the flip-top dispensing cap

blocks.heading: Made to be handled by children
blocks.body: Washable from skin, from clothes and from most hard surfaces with warm water. The flip-top cap meters the pour so a tipped bottle does not empty itself across a table. Adult supervision is still the rule — this is a craft chemical, not a toy — but it is formulated on the assumption that small hands will be holding it.

usage.title: Where a bottle like this actually earns its place
usage.lede: Five situations we hear about constantly. If yours is on this list, the 258 mL bottle is almost certainly the right size to start with.

scenarios.title: Thirty children, forty minutes, one adult
scenarios.body: A single bottle covers a full class set with room to spare, and because the ratio is fixed you are not running between tables rescuing sticky bowls. Teachers tend to buy it for the predictability rather than the chemistry.

scenarios.title: A rainy Saturday that does not end in tears
scenarios.body: The failure mode of kitchen slime is a bowl of sticky white mess and a disappointed child. Removing the measuring step removes the failure. Washable formula means the kitchen table survives too.

scenarios.title: Sensory play and occupational therapy
scenarios.body: Consistent texture batch to batch is the point here — a predictable resistance you can rely on session after session. Unscented and uncoloured by design, so it does not fight with sensory sensitivities.
steps: Adjust firmness with a few extra drops

scenarios.title: Content, kits and craft markets
scenarios.body: If you are producing slime to sell or to film, the variable you cannot afford is the batch that comes out wrong on camera. Fixed ratio, repeatable result, and a case pack that keeps the unit cost sensible.

scenarios.title: Party stations and holiday clubs
scenarios.body: A station that runs itself. Pre-portion the glue, hand over the bottle with an adult on it, and the activity paces itself at roughly three minutes a child.
steps: Bag and label to take home

faq.q: Does it work with clear glue as well as white?
faq.a: Yes. Clear PVA gives a glass-like slime and usually wants a slightly longer rest before kneading.

faq.q: What if the slime is still sticky?
faq.a: Add a few more drops and keep kneading. Stickiness is almost always under-activation, not over-activation.

faq.q: What if it has gone rubbery?
faq.a: Too much activator. A little warm water worked in by hand will bring it back most of the time.
It is formulated for supervised craft use from age 3. Wash hands after handling and keep it out of eyes and mouths.
